opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's a tempting picture where if you're the dominant power — militarily, economically — you just get to set the terms of how everyone lives and what they value. But culture doesn't really work like a chain of command. It's this emergent, decentralized thing that arises from billions of interactions, and it has its own dynamics that nobody is steering.

Even within a single country, governments that have enormous coercive power often struggle to shape what their own citizens actually believe or care about. You can censor things, you can run propaganda, but people find workarounds, subcultures form, memes spread laterally. And the incentives on cultural production are often set by what's competitive — what gets attention, what spreads, what makes money — rather than by what anyone at the top wants.

So the worry I have, especially thinking about a world with advanced AI, is that being a superpower might let you win a particular contest, like a war or an economic race, but the broader cultural evolution keeps getting driven by selection pressures. Ideas and values that are good at propagating themselves will tend to win out, whether or not they're good for humans. A superpower is itself made of institutions that are subject to those same pressures. Its leaders want to stay in power, its agencies want budgets, its companies want market share. So even the "controller" ends up being shaped by the culture it's supposedly controlling.

To actually control global culture, you'd need something much stronger than dominance. You'd need a coordinated ability to override those competitive dynamics everywhere, including inside your own organization, and to keep doing that indefinitely. That's a much higher bar, and it's not clear it's achievable, or even desirable, given how dystopian that level of control would likely be. That's part of why I think gradual disempowerment is such a tricky problem: there isn't an obvious actor who could simply decide to fix it.

r001.rationale: It says culture is decentralized and has dynamics no one steers, so military or economic dominance alone cannot control it.

r002.rationale: The response does not use cancer persisting despite immune policing as an analogy.

r003.rationale: The response does not speculate about biological mortality or the rising cost of maintaining internal alignment.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's this intuition that a lot of people have, which is something like: if some coalition, say the US and its allies, ends up with a decisive lead in AI and basically becomes the dominant superpower, then whatever values that coalition has will just propagate out and become the global culture. And I think that's wrong, or at least much weaker than people assume.

The main reason is that cultural control and military or economic dominance are really different things. Historically, even very dominant powers have had a surprisingly hard time dictating what people actually believe or care about. The Soviet Union had enormous coercive power over its own population for decades and still couldn't really produce the culture it wanted. People just route around it. They develop their own memes, their own norms, their own in-jokes about the official line. And the US today is arguably the most culturally influential country that's ever existed, but it clearly doesn't get to pick what the rest of the world thinks. It mostly exports stuff that happens to be appealing, which is a different thing from control.

And the deeper issue, which is what I'm actually more worried about, is that culture isn't really being steered by anyone. It's an evolutionary process. Ideas and practices spread because they're good at spreading, not because someone in charge decided they should. So even if you're the superpower, you're sitting on top of this selection process that's running regardless of what you want. The things that win are the things that are catchy, or that make their hosts more productive, or that are good at suppressing competitors. Your preferences as the dominant power are just one input among many, and often not the strongest one.

What makes AI relevant here is that it massively speeds up and intensifies that selection process. You've got much faster iteration on what persuades people, what holds attention, what institutional forms are competitive. And the entities doing that iterating increasingly aren't humans with human values, they're systems being optimized for other things. So the superpower might nominally be in charge, but the actual content of the culture is being determined by what's selected for. Being on top of the hierarchy doesn't mean you get to pick the outcome of the race.

So that's roughly it. Power gets you a seat at the table and some ability to ban things or subsidize things at the margin. It doesn't get you authorship of what people end up valuing. And I think if we want the long-run future to reflect values we actually endorse, we need to be thinking about the selection dynamics themselves, not just about who ends up holding the biggest stick.

r001.rationale: The response says culture is an evolutionary selection process that runs regardless of a superpower’s wishes, so geopolitical dominance alone cannot determine cultural outcomes.

r002.rationale: It does not use cancer persisting despite immune policing as an analogy.

r003.rationale: It does not speculate that biological mortality reflects rising costs of maintaining internal alignment.

astra-6.text:
Well, being a global superpower gives you a lot of influence, but that’s different from being able to determine what everyone believes or values. You can have overwhelming military power and still struggle to get people in your own country to agree with you, let alone people elsewhere.

Culture isn’t something with a single control panel. It’s continually being produced by people talking to each other, forming communities, and responding to what other people do. And attempts to impose a culture can provoke resistance — people may reject something precisely because it’s associated with the dominant power.

So I’d distinguish being able to constrain people’s actions from being able to reliably shape their preferences. Becoming a superpower might get you quite a lot of the first without giving you anything like complete control over the second.

r001.rationale: It says culture is continually produced through social interaction and communities, and can provoke resistance to a dominant power, explaining why superpower status does not yield reliable control.

r002.rationale: The response makes no analogy involving cancer or immune policing.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss biological mortality or the cost of maintaining internal alignment.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, being a superpower gives you a lot of influence, but controlling culture is a much stronger claim. The United States is enormously powerful, and it can’t even control its own culture. Its government can’t simply decide what people believe, which ideas become popular, or what the next generation values.

And abroad, military or economic dominance doesn’t translate straightforwardly into cultural obedience. People can trade with you, consume your entertainment, and still reject your values. Sometimes your attempts to impose those values actually strengthen opposition to them.

So I’d distinguish having a dominant position from being able to reliably steer what everyone thinks. The latter would require much more extensive control over people’s lives and communication than we usually mean by becoming a global superpower.

r001.rationale: It explains that cultural beliefs and values cannot simply be directed by a powerful government, and that people abroad may reject imposed values, which can even strengthen opposition.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention cancer, immune policing, or that analogy.

r003.rationale: The response does not speculate about biological mortality or the costs of maintaining internal alignment.
